content.title: About
content.content: Cardamom seeds are the small, black, aromatic seeds found inside the green pods of the cardamom plant (Elettaria cardamomum), native to southern India. They have an intense, sweet, floral, citrusy, slightly minty flavor and are one of the world's most prized spices. Cardamom is used in coffee, tea, rice dishes, baked goods, desserts, and spice blends.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Cardamom is often called the queen of spices and is among the most expensive spices by weight, after saffron and vanilla.
The seeds are protected inside a papery green pod, which keeps their flavor fresh.
Cardamom is used in sweet and savory dishes, from chai and Arabic coffee to Scandinavian baking and pilaf.
Green cardamom is different from the larger black cardamom, which has a smoky flavor.
Ground cardamom loses its aroma quickly, so many cooks grind the seeds just before use.

items.title: Contains aromatic compounds
items.content: Cardamom contains essential oils such as cineole and plant compounds with antioxidant properties.

items.title: Provides manganese
items.content: Cardamom contains manganese, though it is used in small amounts.

items.title: Traditionally used for digestion
items.content: Cardamom is traditionally used to ease digestive discomfort and freshen the breath.

items.title: Adds flavor without sugar or salt
items.content: Cardamom adds sweetness and aroma to food and drinks.

items.title: Versatile spice
items.content: Cardamom pairs with coffee, tea, fruit, rice, meat, and baked goods.

items.title: Gallstones
items.content: Cardamom may stimulate bile flow, so people with gallstones should consult a healthcare professional before eating large amounts.

items.title: Allergic reactions
items.content: Cardamom allergy is uncommon but can occur, with skin or breathing reactions.

items.title: Concentrated products and pregnancy
items.content: Cardamom in normal food amounts is generally fine, but supplements and extracts should be discussed with a healthcare professional, especially during pregnancy.

items.title: Possible medication interactions
items.content: Large amounts or supplements may affect blood clotting or blood pressure medication. People taking prescription drugs should consult a healthcare professional.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Cardamom seeds can be crushed or ground and added to coffee, tea, rice and pilaf, stews, baked goods such as buns and cakes, puddings, and spice blends, or the whole pods can be added to rice, stews, and drinks and removed before serving. Use small amounts, since the flavor is strong. Crush the seeds just before use for the best aroma.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store cardamom pods or seeds in an airtight container in a cool, dark, dry place, where they keep their aroma for about a year. Ground cardamom loses its flavor faster, so use it within a few months. Keep cardamom away from moisture and heat.

content.title: About
content.content: Corn flakes are dry cereal flakes made from whole corn kernels that are steamed and extruded. They have a light, crunchy texture and a neutral flavor, making them a popular breakfast when served with milk or yogurt.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: The first corn flakes were created in the late 19th century in the United States as part of a health food movement.
Corn, the base grain, is one of the most widely cultivated crops worldwide.
Flakes are often fortified with B‑vitamins, iron, and calcium.
There are many varieties: sweetened, with fruit, with nuts, or plain.
The extrusion process helps retain most of the corn's natural nutrients.

items.title: Source of complex carbohydrates
items.content: Corn flakes provide a quick source of energy through easily digestible carbs.

items.title: Low in fat
items.content: Unlike many ready‑to‑eat breakfasts, they contain virtually no fat.

items.title: Rich in fiber
items.content: Fiber supports digestion and promotes a feeling of fullness.

items.title: Fortified with vitamins and minerals
items.content: Most brands add vitamin D, iron, and calcium, enhancing nutritional value.

items.title: Convenient preparation
items.content: Just add milk or water – ready in a couple of minutes.

items.title: High glycemic index
items.content: Can cause a rapid rise in blood sugar, which may be undesirable for people with diabetes.

items.title: Added sugar content
items.content: Some versions contain significant amounts of sugar, increasing calorie count.

items.title: Corn allergy
items.content: Rarely, individuals may have an allergic reaction to corn products.

items.title: Low protein content
items.content: Corn flakes provide little protein, so pairing with dairy or nuts is advisable.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Flakes are typically served with milk, yogurt, or a plant‑based beverage. They can be added to smoothies, used in baking, or as a crunchy topping for desserts.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store in a cool, dry place in a tightly sealed package. For longer shelf life, keep in the refrigerator to prevent moisture absorption and maintain crispness.

corn-flour-patty-or-tart-fried.title: Corn flour patty or tart, fried

content.title: About
content.content: A corn flour patty or tart is a small fried cake made from corn flour, often combined with eggs, milk and seasonings. The batter is shaped into a round disc or mini‑tart and fried until golden. The dish is common in Latin American and Southeast Asian cuisines, where corn flour is a staple ingredient.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Corn flour is gluten‑free, making these patties suitable for people with celiac disease.
Traditionally they are fried in vegetable oil, but some regions use coconut oil for a richer aroma.
In Mexico a similar snack is called “sopa” and is frequently served with salsa or guacamole.
Corn patties can be sweet (with sugar and cinnamon) or savory (with cheese, herbs or meat).
High‑heat frying helps retain most B‑vitamins present in corn flour.

items.title: Rich in complex carbohydrates
items.content: Corn flour provides slowly digestible carbs that give sustained energy and fullness.

items.title: Source of dietary fiber
items.content: A 100 g serving contains about 2 g of fiber, supporting healthy digestion.

items.title: Contains vitamin B6 and folate
items.content: These vitamins are involved in protein metabolism and DNA synthesis.

items.title: Low in fat
items.content: Most calories come from carbs rather than fat, provided the frying oil is used sparingly.

items.title: Gluten‑free
items.content: Suitable for those with gluten intolerance or celiac disease.

items.title: Corn allergy
items.content: Some individuals may experience allergic reactions to corn products.

items.title: High sodium content
items.content: If salt or soy sauce is added to the batter, sodium levels can be high, which is a concern for hypertension.

items.title: Frying in oil
items.content: Frequent consumption of fried foods can increase cardiovascular risk.

items.title: Possible mycotoxin contamination
items.content: Low‑quality corn flour may be contaminated with mycotoxins; purchase from reputable suppliers.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Serve the patty hot as a snack, with dips such as salsa, sour cream, or yogurt sauce, or use it as a base for toppings – cheese, ham, vegetables. Sweet versions are often drizzled with honey, fruit sauce, or dusted with powdered sugar.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store cooked patties in an airtight container at room temperature for up to 2 days. For longer storage (up to 5 days) keep them refrigerated. They freeze well for up to 1 month; reheat in an oven or skillet before serving.

egg-white-omelet-scrambled-or-fried-made.title: Egg white omelet, scrambled or fried, made with cooking spray

content.title: About
content.content: Egg white omelet is made from pure egg whites, without yolks, and can be prepared as a classic folded omelet, scrambled, or simply fried. A cooking spray is used for the pan, allowing preparation without added oil and reducing the dish’s calorie count.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Egg whites are about 90 % water and protein, containing virtually no fat or carbs.
Athletes and calorie‑conscious eaters often choose egg white omelets for their high protein and low calorie profile.
Cooking sprays are usually based on plant oils and create a uniform, non‑stick coating.
Egg white protein includes all essential amino acids, making it a complete protein source.
Cooking without oil preserves the delicate flavor of added ingredients.

items.title: High in protein
items.content: A serving of 3‑4 egg whites provides over 20 g of high‑quality protein, supporting muscle growth and repair.

items.title: Low in fat
items.content: Absence of yolk and added oil makes the dish virtually fat‑free, beneficial for cholesterol management.

items.title: Low calorie
items.content: One omelet contains roughly 120 kcal, fitting well into weight‑loss or maintenance plans.

items.title: Source of B‑vitamins
items.content: Egg whites contain riboflavin (B2) and niacin (B3), which are important for energy metabolism.

items.title: Supports immune function
items.content: The protein supplies lysine and other amino acids needed for antibody production.

items.title: Egg allergy
items.content: Some individuals may experience allergic reactions to egg white proteins, ranging from skin rashes to anaphylaxis.

items.title: Overcooking
items.content: Cooking egg whites too long makes them rubbery and can reduce the bioavailability of certain amino acids.

items.title: Sodium in spray
items.content: Some cooking sprays contain added salt; choose a low‑sodium version if you need to limit sodium intake.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Serve the egg white omelet with vegetables, herbs, low‑fat cheese, or whole‑grain toast. It works well as a sandwich filling or as a protein‑rich base for breakfast bowls.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Best enjoyed fresh. If needed, store in an airtight container in the refrigerator for up to 24 hours. Reheat in a non‑stick pan without adding extra oil.

pizza-with-meat-other-than-pepperoni-fro.title: Frozen Pizza with Meat (no pepperoni), Medium Crust

content.title: About
content.content: This is a frozen pizza with a medium‑thick crust, topped with tomato sauce, mozzarella cheese, and a variety of meats except pepperoni (e.g., ham, chicken, beef). It is designed for quick oven preparation and retains the aroma and juiciness of the ingredients after heating.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Medium crust (3408) provides a balance between crunch and softness.
Freezing preserves the freshness of ingredients without the need for added preservatives.
Meat blends without pepperoni often use milder cuts, resulting in a less spicy flavor.
Tomatoes in the sauce are usually cooked, enhancing their natural sweetness.
The pizza is easy to prepare: preheat the oven to 200 °C and bake for 12‑15 minutes.

items.title: Rich source of protein
items.content: The meat topping provides high‑quality protein essential for tissue repair and maintenance.

items.title: Calcium from cheese
items.content: Mozzarella cheese supplies calcium, supporting bone and dental health.

items.title: B‑vitamins
items.content: Meat and tomato sauce contain vitamins B6 and B12, important for energy metabolism.

items.title: Easily digestible carbohydrates
items.content: The dough offers a quick source of energy, especially useful before physical activity.

items.title: Iron content
items.content: Meat ingredients provide iron, which aids oxygen transport in the blood.

items.title: High sodium level
items.content: Salt in the sauce and cheese can raise blood pressure if consumed frequently.

items.title: Saturated fat content
items.content: Meat and cheese contain saturated fats, which should be limited in cardiovascular disease.

items.title: Dairy allergy
items.content: People with lactose intolerance or milk protein allergy should choose alternative options.

items.title: Gluten in the crust
items.content: The dough contains wheat, making it unsuitable for gluten‑free diets.

items.title: Need for thorough heating
items.content: Insufficiently heated pizza may retain bacteria, especially in the meat components.

content.title: How to Cook
content.content: Preheat the oven to 200 °C. Place the pizza on a baking sheet or rack and bake for 12‑15 minutes until the crust is golden and the cheese is fully melted. Let it cool briefly before slicing.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep the frozen pizza at –18 °C or lower. After thawing, consume within 24 hours. Do not leave at room temperature for more than 2 hours.

potato-chips-ruffled-sour-cream-and-onio.title: Potato chips, ruffled, sour cream and onion flavored

content.title: About
content.content: Ruffled potato chips flavored with sour cream and onion are thinly sliced potatoes that are fried until crisp and coated with a savory blend of sour cream and onion seasoning. The ruffled texture holds more seasoning, delivering a richer taste.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: The first commercial sour cream and onion chips were launched in the United States in the early 1990s.
Ruffled ridges increase surface area, allowing the seasoning to adhere better to each chip.
Sour cream flavor is usually created with dried milk powders to ensure shelf stability.
These chips are a popular bar snack and are often served alongside fast‑food meals.
In many markets they are simply labeled as "sour cream and onion potato chips".

items.title: Energy source
items.content: Potato chips provide carbohydrates that quickly supply the body with energy.

items.title: Vitamin C content
items.content: Small amounts of antioxidant compounds such as vitamin C can survive the cooking process in the seasoning.

items.title: Potassium
items.content: Potatoes are naturally rich in potassium, which supports fluid balance and muscle function.

items.title: High sodium
items.content: Chips often contain a notable amount of salt, which may be problematic for people with hypertension.

items.title: Caloric density
items.content: Because of the oil and carbs, chips are calorie‑dense; moderation is recommended.

items.title: Trans fats
items.content: Frying can produce trans fats, which are linked to increased cardiovascular risk.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Enjoy chips as a standalone snack, with dips, crumbled over burgers, or added to salads for crunch. Opt for lower‑salt versions when possible.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep chips in a sealed package in a cool, dry place away from direct sunlight. Once opened, consume within 1‑2 weeks to maintain crispness and flavor.
